Title: Officers who captured Charleston church shooter speak out for 1st time: ‘It was like staring Satan in the...
SHELBY, N.C. (WBTV) - Police officers in Shelby, North Carolina, joked in 2015 that a 21-year-old who murdered nine people at a church 250 miles away would come through their small town.
Sergeant Mike Myers, Sergeant Dan Bernat, and officer Scott Hamrick did not anticipate, however, that they’d be the ones to take Dylann Roof into custody.
Roof, 21, murdered nine Black parishioners at the Mother Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina on June 17, 2015.

For the first time since the massacre, three of the five officers who detained Roof in Shelby spoke exclusively with WBTV about how an ordinary day turned into one that helped bring a conclusion to a horrific act of hate.
Roof was nowhere to be found after the deadly mass shooting on Wednesday, June 17, 2015.
The following morning, there was a possible sighting in Shelby, North Carolina.
“It all started with one woman who paid attention,” said former Shelby police chief, Jeff Ledford.
That woman was Debra Dills.
She was on her way to work when she noticed someone who looked like Dylann Roof driving a black Hyundai Elantra.
Dills called her boss, who called someone at the Kings Mountain Police Department, who then called the Shelby Police Department.
At 10:32 a.m. on that Thursday, a radio call was made to Shelby police officers.
Bernat tried to pull up a picture of Roof on his cell phone, his partner Officer Burris spotted the black Hyundai.
They followed the car west down U.S. 74 near Polkville Road.
Officer Scott Hamrick and Sgt.
Mike Myers joined the pursuit.
Bernat made the call.
“It had to be done, it had to be effective, it had to be then,” Sgt.
Bernat said.
He turned on his blue lights, and the black Hyundai pulled off U.S. 74 at Plato Lee Road into a driveway of an abandoned home.
Officer Burris and Sgt.
Bernat got out of their car as Hamrick was behind them with his gun drawn, pointed at the driver.
Bernat approached the car, he said one thought went through his mind: the driver appeared to be a child.
At 10:49 a.m., Roof was put in handcuffs.
He complied with officers and admitted what he had done.
“I remember me asking him, ‘What’s your name?’ And he said, ‘Dylann Roof.’ I said, ‘Were you involved in the shooting in Charleston at the church?’ And he said, ‘yes,’” Sgt.
Myers said.
Myers then asked Roof if there were any weapons in the car.
Roof admitted there was a gun in the back seat.
But how Roof referred to the weapon grabbed Sgt.
Myer’s attention.
“He referred to it as the gun.
It stuck out to me when he said, ‘The gun is in the back seat under the pillow.’ It wasn’t ‘there’s a gun,’ it was ‘the gun,’” Sgt.
Myers said.
Officer Hamrick then drove Roof to the Shelby Police Department.
Myers said Roof didn’t show any remorse.
Jeff Ledford said he was being interviewed by a reporter for an unrelated story when he heard what his officers had accomplished.
Despite their efforts, Shelby police drew criticism online following Roof’s arrest.
Did officers really buy Roof food from Burger King?
“That got blown way out of proportion,” Ledford said.
Ledford said he got a phone call from a reporter who asked the following questions about someone in custody: Did they ask for an attorney?
Did they need food?
Did they ask for anything to eat?
Did you feed them?
Ledford believes his answer was misconstrued.
Ledford explained that community members had brought food from several different fast-food restaurants to the Shelby Police Department to show their appreciation.
An article from a local media outlet said: “Earlier in the day, Roof had bought water and chips at a south Charlotte gas station.
Now he was hungry.
Police bought him food from a nearby Burger King,” Ledford said.
“National outlets picked out that one line from a bigger story and ran with it.
Social media helped spread the misinformation faster -- some believed the officers took Roof inside the fast-food restaurant and ate at a booth with him.
Others believed the officers took Roof through a the drive-thru.
All of that is false, according to Ledford.
“I can assure that you at no point did any of that ever happen,” Ledford said.
Officer Hamrick backed up his statement.
“I can assure you that I did not take him to Burger King before I took him back to the [police station],” officer Hamrick said.
Myers said he and his fellow officers also received criticism for how they reacted after apprehending Roof.
In dash camera video, the officers were seen giving each other fist bumps and high fives.
Myers said he and his fellow officers conducted themselves in a way that didn’t cause Roof to react.
“I was thinking about what he might do.
I knew what I was going to do if he did something, but fortunately that didn’t happen,” officer Hamrick said.
Bernat, Sgt.
Myers, and officer Hamrick all testified at Roof’s trial.
He was convicted of 33 federal hate crime charges and sentenced to death.
“The justice system … it did work here in the flesh.
Judgement to me will be in [Roof’s] next life.
I think that’s when he’ll receive true judgement,” Sgt.
Bernat said.
All the officers agree that witnessing the guilty verdict was satisfying for them and the families of the victims.
“They got to look the devil in the eyes, the families did,” Sgt.
Myers said.
The officers who arrested Roof have been called heroes, but each of them said that it’s a title they don’t want.
The officers -- all downplaying their role in bringing justice to the families of the nine victims -- humbly redirected the focus to Charleston, South Carolina.
“We only had a small part,” said Sgt.
WBTV will be sharing several stories related to the 2015 massacre at the Charleston church on Tuesday, June 17.
